c-tr-classify.label: Acute, right or obtuse from the three sides
c-tr-classify.summary: Compare the square of the longest side with the sum of the squares of the other two — that alone tells you the triangle's angle type.

q-tr-classify.label: Decide acute / right / obtuse from three side lengths or a ratio
q-tr-classify.summary: Given three sides (or a ratio of sides), say whether the triangle is acute-, right- or obtuse-angled.

c-tr-cevian.label: Medians, bisectors and parallel-line segments
c-tr-cevian.summary: Special segments inside a triangle — medians (meeting at the centroid, split 2:1), the angle bisector (splits the opposite side in the ratio of the adjacent sides), and any line parallel to a side (cuts the other two sides in the same ratio).

q-tr-median-hyp.label: Median to the hypotenuse of a right triangle
q-tr-median-hyp.summary: The median from the right angle to the hypotenuse is always half the hypotenuse.

q-tr-equilateral-seg.label: Inradius, circumradius and median of an equilateral triangle
q-tr-equilateral-seg.summary: In an equilateral triangle these three special lengths are all fixed multiples of each other.

q-tr-median-perp.label: Two medians meeting at right angles
q-tr-median-perp.summary: Split each median 2 : 1 at the centroid, then use the right angle between them with Pythagoras.

q-tr-bisector.label: Internal bisector splitting the opposite side
q-tr-bisector.summary: An internal angle bisector splits the opposite side in the same ratio as the two adjacent sides.

q-tr-parallel.label: Basic proportionality (Thales) theorem
q-tr-parallel.summary: A line parallel to one side of a triangle cuts the other two sides proportionally — use it to find a missing segment.

c-tr-centers.label: Incentre, circumcentre and orthocentre
c-tr-centers.summary: The incentre gives a clean angle formula (∠BOC = 90° + A/2). Where the orthocentre or circumcentre sits (inside, on a vertex/side, or outside) tells you the triangle's type.

q-tr-incentre.label: ∠BOC = 90° + A/2 at the incentre
q-tr-incentre.summary: Given two angles (or the vertex angle A directly), find the angle the incentre makes with the other two vertices, or run the formula backwards.

q-tr-center-facts.label: What a centre's special position tells you
q-tr-center-facts.summary: Orthocentre = centroid ⟺ equilateral. Orthocentre on a vertex ⟺ right-angled there. Circumcentre outside ⟺ obtuse.

formulas.text: For sides a ≤ b ≤ c: c² < a² + b² acute, c² = a² + b² right-angled, c² > a² + b² obtuse
formulas.note: Only the longest side's square needs comparing — the common factor in a ratio like 3:4:6 cancels out.

formulas.text: In a right triangle, the median from the right-angle vertex to the hypotenuse = half the hypotenuse
formulas.note: Equivalent to: the right-angle vertex lies on the circle with the hypotenuse as diameter, and the median is a radius.

formulas.text: Equilateral triangle: circumradius R = 2 × inradius r; and r = (median)/3 (the centroid splits each median 2 : 1)
formulas.note: So a median = 3r = 1.5R — any one of the three (side, R, r, median) gives the other three.

formulas.text: The centroid splits every median 2 : 1 from the vertex
formulas.note: Needed whenever a question gives a whole median's length but the working needs the centroid's two pieces separately (e.g. two perpendicular medians).

formulas.text: Angle bisector theorem: if AD bisects ∠A meeting BC at D, then BD : DC = AB : AC
formulas.note: Works in either direction — from the side ratio to BD/DC, or from BD/DC to the side ratio.

formulas.text: Basic proportionality (Thales) theorem: if PQ ∥ BC with P on AB and Q on AC, then AP/PB = AQ/QC, and also AP/AB = AQ/AC = PQ/BC
formulas.note: Pick whichever of the two ratio forms matches what the question gives — part:part, or part:whole.
Works forwards (given angles, find the incentre angle) or backwards (given the incentre angle, find a vertex angle).

formulas.text: Orthocentre = centroid ⟺ the triangle is equilateral. Orthocentre lies on a vertex ⟺ the triangle is right-angled there. Circumcentre lies outside the triangle ⟺ the triangle is obtuse-angled
formulas.note: All four classical centres (centroid, incentre, circumcentre, orthocentre) coincide only in the equilateral case.

q-tr-classify.cue: 'The sides of a triangle are … (or are in the ratio …). The triangle is:' with acute/right/obtuse as options.
q-tr-classify.standard: Square the largest side and compare it with the sum of the squares of the other two.
q-tr-classify.fast: With a ratio, just compare the squares of the ratio numbers directly — the scale factor cancels.
q-tr-classify.eliminate: If the comparison is close to equal, check for a Pythagorean triple (3-4-5, 6-8-10, 5-12-13, …) first.
traps: Comparing the wrong side as 'largest'.
Mixing up the inequality direction (bigger sum-of-squares means acute, not obtuse).
Forgetting a ratio's common factor cancels, so the raw ratio numbers can be compared directly.

q-tr-median-hyp.cue: Three side lengths are given (often a Pythagorean triple) and the question asks for the median to the largest/greatest side.
q-tr-median-hyp.standard: Confirm the triangle is right-angled (largest² = sum of other two squares), then the median to the hypotenuse is simply half of it.
q-tr-median-hyp.fast: Recognise the triple (6-8-10, 3-4-5, 5-12-13, …) on sight — the median is then just half the largest number.
q-tr-median-hyp.eliminate: The answer must be exactly half the given largest side; rule out anything that isn't.
traps: Giving a leg's length instead of half the hypotenuse.
Computing the altitude to the hypotenuse (leg₁×leg₂/hypotenuse) instead of the median.
Not checking first that the triangle actually is right-angled.

q-tr-equilateral-seg.cue: 'Circumradius of an equilateral triangle is …, find the inradius' or '…inradius is …, find the median' (or side).
q-tr-equilateral-seg.standard: Use R = 2r and r = median/3 to convert directly between whichever two of {R, r, median, side} the question involves.
q-tr-equilateral-seg.fast: Memorise the chain: median = 3r = 1.5R — one multiplication or division solves it.
q-tr-equilateral-seg.eliminate: r must be smaller than R (specifically R = 2r exactly) and smaller than the median (r = median/3) — options that break this ratio are wrong.
traps: Mixing up which of R and r is bigger (R is always twice r, never the other way round).
Using the general-triangle inradius formula (Area/semi-perimeter) when the direct equilateral-triangle ratio is much faster.
Confusing the median with the full height split 1:1 instead of 2:1.

q-tr-median-perp.cue: Two medians are given to intersect 'at right angles' (or 'perpendicularly') at the centroid, and a segment like BD (half a side) is asked for.
q-tr-median-perp.standard: Split each median 2 : 1 at the centroid to get the two legs of a right triangle at G, then apply Pythagoras for the needed side.
q-tr-median-perp.fast: Once the two centroid-pieces come out as a recognisable triple (like 3-4-5), the hypotenuse is immediate.
q-tr-median-perp.eliminate: Using the full medians as the right-triangle legs (instead of their 2:1 pieces) gives a much bigger, wrong number — a good sign the split was skipped.
traps: Using the whole median lengths as the legs instead of splitting 2:1 at the centroid.
Mixing up which piece (2/3 or 1/3) belongs to which vertex.
Forgetting BD is HALF of BC, not the full side, if BC itself were asked for instead.

q-tr-bisector.cue: 'AD is the internal bisector of ∠A, meeting BC at D' with two of BD, DC, BC given, asking for AB : AC (or vice versa).
q-tr-bisector.standard: Find the missing piece of BC if needed (BC − given piece), then AB : AC = BD : DC directly.
q-tr-bisector.fast: If BD and BC are given, DC = BC − BD falls out in one subtraction before applying the theorem.
q-tr-bisector.eliminate: The ratio must simplify the same way BD : DC does — options that don't reduce to that exact ratio are wrong.
traps: Inverting the ratio (DC : BD instead of BD : DC, or vice versa, depending which side the question asks first).
Using BD : BC or DC : BC instead of BD : DC.
Forgetting to subtract from BC to get the missing piece before forming the ratio.

q-tr-parallel.cue: 'A line parallel to BC intersects AB and AC at P and Q' with a mix of segment lengths given, one of which may be unknown and shared with another via a condition like AP = QC.
q-tr-parallel.standard: Write the proportion AP/PB = AQ/QC (or the part:whole form AP/AB = AQ/AC = PQ/BC, whichever matches what's given) and solve for the unknown.
q-tr-parallel.fast: When the unknown appears on both sides of the proportion (like AP = QC), it often collapses to a mean-proportional square root.
q-tr-parallel.eliminate: A ratio answer (like 'AC = 3×AQ') should be checked by confirming AP:AB equals the same ratio as AQ:AC — if not, the wrong pair of segments was used.
traps: Mixing up the part:part form (AP/PB) with the part:whole form (AP/AB).
Using the wrong vertex's segments (B's instead of C's, or vice versa).
Not spotting a mean-proportional setup when the same unknown appears in two places.

q-tr-incentre.cue: 'I (or O) is the incentre of △ABC' with either two base angles given (find ∠BIC) or the vertex angle A given (find ∠BOC), or the reverse (∠BOC given, find ∠A).
q-tr-incentre.standard: Find ∠A (from 180° minus the other two, if not given directly), then apply ∠BOC = 90° + ∠A/2 — or solve this same equation for ∠A if ∠BOC is what's given.
q-tr-incentre.fast: If ∠A is given directly, skip the triangle-angle-sum step entirely and halve it straight into the formula.
q-tr-incentre.eliminate: ∠BOC must always be between 90° and 180° (since 0° < A < 180°) — an option outside that range is wrong immediately.
traps: Using ∠A alone, or ∠A/2 alone, instead of 90° + ∠A/2.
Forgetting to subtract from 180° to get ∠A when only the other two angles are given.
When running the formula backwards, forgetting to double (∠A/2 vs ∠A) after subtracting 90°.

q-tr-center-facts.cue: A qualitative fact about where a named centre (orthocentre, circumcentre) sits — 'the orthocentre and centroid are the same', 'the orthocentre lies on a vertex', 'the circumcentre lies outside the triangle' — asking for the triangle's type.
q-tr-center-facts.standard: Match the stated position directly to the known fact: centres coincide ⟺ equilateral; orthocentre on a vertex ⟺ right-angled there; circumcentre outside ⟺ obtuse-angled.
q-tr-center-facts.fast: These are pure recall — no computation, just matching the position to the triangle type.
q-tr-center-facts.eliminate: A scalene or isosceles option (with nothing more specific stated) is never the match for any of these special positions.
traps: Confusing the orthocentre's special positions with the circumcentre's (they are opposite in the obtuse case: orthocentre moves further outside, circumcentre also outside, but 'on a vertex' is specifically an orthocentre/right-angle fact).
Thinking any isosceles triangle has coinciding centres — only equilateral does.
Mixing up 'inside' (acute) and 'outside' (obtuse) for the circumcentre.

pyqs.text: The sides of a triangle are in the ratio 3 : 4 : 6. The triangle is:
solution: Compare the square of the largest side (6k)² = 36k² with the sum of the other two squares (3k)² + (4k)² = 9k² + 16k² = 25k².
36k² > 25k², so the angle opposite the largest side is obtuse.
pyqs.trick: Just compare 6² with 3² + 4²: 36 against 25. Bigger means obtuse, no angle computation needed.

pyqs.text: If the length of the three sides of a triangle are 6 cm, 8 cm and 10 cm, then the length of the median to its greatest side is
solution: 6² + 8² = 36 + 64 = 100 = 10², so the triangle is right-angled with hypotenuse 10 cm.
The median to the hypotenuse of a right triangle equals half the hypotenuse: 10/2 = 5 cm.
pyqs.trick: Spot the 6-8-10 triple first — then the median to the hypotenuse is just half of 10.

pyqs.text: If the circumradius of an equilateral triangle be 10 cm, then the measure of its in-radius is
solution: For an equilateral triangle the circumcentre and incentre coincide, and the circumradius is always twice the inradius: R = 2r.
pyqs.trick: Equilateral triangle shortcut: inradius is always exactly half the circumradius.

b.note: Repeated the circumradius instead of halving it.

c.note: Doubled the circumradius instead of halving it.

pyqs.text: The in-radius of an equilateral triangle is of length 3 cm. Then the length of each of its medians is
solution: In an equilateral triangle the centroid (= incentre) splits every median 2 : 1 from the vertex, so the inradius is the 1/3 share nearest the base: r = (median)/3.
median = 3r = 3 × 3 = 9 cm.
pyqs.trick: Inradius is exactly 1/3 of a median in an equilateral triangle — multiply by 3 to invert it.

b.note: Divided 9 by 2 by confusing it with a different ratio.

c.note: Added 1 to the inradius instead of multiplying by 3.

pyqs.text: Two medians AD and BE of △ABC intersect at G at right angles. If AD = 9 cm and BE = 6 cm, then the length of BD (in cm) is
solution: The centroid G divides each median 2 : 1 from the vertex: AG = (2/3)(9) = 6, GD = (1/3)(9) = 3, BG = (2/3)(6) = 4, GE = (1/3)(6) = 2.
Since AD ⊥ BE at G, triangle BGD is right-angled at G, with legs BG = 4 and GD = 3.
pyqs.trick: Split each median 2 : 1 at the centroid first, then it's a plain 3-4-5 right triangle at G.

a.note: Not √(BG²+GD²) for the centroid-split legs — does not match the right computation.

b.note: Took BD as equal to BE.

d.note: Took BD as the short centroid piece GD alone.

pyqs.text: In △ABC, AD is the internal bisector of ∠A, meeting the side BC at D. If BD = 5 cm, BC = 7.5 cm, then AB : AC is
solution: By the angle bisector theorem, AB : AC = BD : DC = 5 : 2.5 = 2 : 1.
pyqs.trick: The bisector theorem turns this straight into a side ratio — no triangle construction needed, just BD : DC.

pyqs.text: A straight line parallel to BC of △ABC intersects AB and AC at points P and Q respectively. AP = QC, PB = 4 units and AQ = 9 units, then the length of AP is:
solution: By the basic proportionality theorem, AP/PB = AQ/QC.
Let AP = QC = x (given). Then x/4 = 9/x, so x² = 36, x = 6.
pyqs.trick: AP = QC turns the proportion into x/4 = 9/x, i.e. x = √(4×9) — a mean-proportional shortcut.

a.note: Not the mean-proportional root √(4×9) — does not match the right computation.

pyqs.text: The points D and E are taken on the sides AB and AC of △ABC such that AD = (1/3)AB, AE = (1/3)AC. If the length of BC is 15 cm, then the length of DE is:
solution: AD/AB = AE/AC = 1/3 with the shared angle A, so triangles ADE and ABC are similar (SAS) and DE ∥ BC.
DE/BC = AD/AB = 1/3, so DE = 15/3 = 5 cm.
pyqs.trick: DE : BC is exactly the same ratio as AD : AB — here 1 : 3 — so DE = BC/3 directly.

a.note: Took DE as 2/3 of BC instead of 1/3.

pyqs.text: In △ABC, PQ is parallel to BC. If AP : PB = 1 : 2 and AQ = 3 cm, AC is equal to
solution: AP : PB = 1 : 2 ⟹ AP : AB = 1 : 3.
By the basic proportionality theorem, AQ : AC = AP : AB = 1 : 3, so AC = 3 × AQ = 3 × 3 = 9 cm.
pyqs.trick: Convert the part-to-part ratio AP:PB=1:2 into the part-to-whole ratio AP:AB=1:3 first, then scale AQ by 3.

pyqs.trick: Same incentre formula, used the other way round: straight from ∠A with nothing else needed.

solution: All four classical centres (centroid, incentre, circumcentre, orthocentre) coincide at a single point only for an equilateral triangle.
So the orthocentre and centroid can be equal only when the triangle is equilateral.
pyqs.trick: Memorise the fact directly: centres coinciding ⟺ equilateral.

pyqs.text: If in a triangle, the orthocentre lies on vertex, then the triangle is
solution: The orthocentre sits inside an acute triangle, outside an obtuse triangle, and exactly AT the right-angle vertex of a right triangle.
So the orthocentre lying on a vertex means the triangle is right-angled there.
pyqs.trick: Orthocentre position is a direct triangle-type indicator: inside/outside/on-vertex ↔ acute/obtuse/right.

pyqs.text: If the circumcentre of a triangle lies outside it, then the triangle is
solution: The circumcentre lies inside an acute triangle, on the midpoint of the hypotenuse of a right triangle (on the boundary), and outside an obtuse triangle.
So lying strictly outside means the triangle is obtuse-angled.
pyqs.trick: Same family of fact as the orthocentre one: circumcentre inside/on-side/outside ↔ acute/right/obtuse.
